ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a battery, and on the current path it first passes through bulb #1, then reaches a junction. From this junction downward there is bulb #2 connected to the bottom return line; to the right there is a branch containing bulb #3 connected to the right-side return line; above there is also a branch containing bulb #4 and switch S, and only when switch S is closed is the bulb #4 branch connected. Therefore, #1 is in series in the total circuit, and #2, #3, and #4 after closing form parallel branches. Reasoning: Let the resistance of each identical bulb be R, and brightness corresponds to the power dissipated by the bulb. When the switch is open, #4 is not powered, #2 and #3 are in parallel, the equivalent resistance is R||R=R/2, and the total resistance is R+R/2=3R/2. After the switch is closed, #2, #3, and #4 are three in parallel, the equivalent resistance is R||R||R=R/3, and the total resistance is R+R/3=4R/3. The total resistance decreases, so the total current through the series bulb #1 increases, the power I^2R of #1 increases, and therefore #1 becomes brighter. The voltage of the parallel part drops from E/3 when the switch is open to E/4 after closing, so #2 and #3 will not become brighter, but instead become dimmer. #4 is lit, but the question asks which other bulb becomes brighter.

method.method_draft: Use an equivalent-resistance comparison before and after the switch closes. From the image, identify bulb #1 as lying in series between the battery and a junction. From that junction to the return wire, bulb #2 is one branch, bulb #3 is another branch, and bulb #4 becomes an additional branch only when switch S is closed. From the text, use that all bulbs are identical, so assign each resistance R, and interpret brightness as electrical power dissipated. With S open, the load after bulb #1 is R || R = R/2, so total resistance is R + R/2 = 3R/2. With S closed, the load after bulb #1 is R || R || R = R/3, so total resistance is R + R/3 = 4R/3. The total current through the series bulb #1 therefore increases, so bulb #1 gets brighter. The voltage across the parallel bank decreases from E/3 to E/4, so bulbs #2 and #3 do not become brighter. Bulb #4 turns on, but the question asks which other bulb becomes brighter, so the answer is bulb #1 only.

method.method_draft: Use a node-voltage/Kirchhoff-current viewpoint. From the image, label the junction after bulb #1 as node A and the bottom/right wire as the return node. Bulb #1 connects the battery to node A; bulbs #2 and #3 connect node A to the return node; closing S adds bulb #4 as a third identical connection from node A to the return node. From the text, treat all bulbs as equal resistors and compare brightness by voltage or current. Let the battery emf be E. Before closing, current leaving node A through two equal bulbs is 2V_A/R, and the current through bulb #1 is (E - V_A)/R, so Kirchhoff’s law gives (E - V_A)/R = 2V_A/R, hence V_A = E/3. After closing, current leaving node A is 3V_A/R, so (E - V_A)/R = 3V_A/R, hence V_A = E/4. Thus the voltage across bulbs #2 and #3 falls, so they dim. The voltage across bulb #1 rises from E - E/3 = 2E/3 to E - E/4 = 3E/4, so bulb #1 dissipates more power and becomes brighter. Therefore the only other bulb that becomes brighter is #1.
